notes.meaning: At daybreak, the chief priests and Jewish elders held a formal meeting to plan how to put Jesus to death. They had already condemned him during the night, but now they gathered at dawn to confirm their decision legally. Because they lacked the power under Roman rule to carry out an execution, they plotted to bring political charges against him.

The leaders tied Jesus' hands and led him through the streets as a criminal. They handed him over to Pontius Pilate, the Roman governor of Judea, so that Rome would carry out the death sentence. This fulfilled Jesus' earlier words that he would be handed over to Gentile rulers.

When Judas saw that Jesus was condemned to die, he was struck with sudden horror and regret. He may have expected Jesus to escape or perform a miracle to save himself. In deep anguish, he tried to return the thirty silver coins to the chief priests and elders.

Judas openly admitted that he had sinned by handing over an innocent person to die. The Jewish leaders coldly brushed him aside, telling him that his guilt was his own concern. Judas's desperate confession gave clear proof from an insider that Jesus had done nothing wrong.

Judas threw the silver coins right onto the temple sanctuary floor and fled. Crushed by despair and the fear of God's wrath, he went away and hanged himself. His deep remorse drove him to self-destruction instead of turning to God for mercy and true forgiveness.

The chief priests gathered the coins from the floor. They recognized that the money had paid for a man's death, so it was unlawful to put it into the holy temple treasury. Even while arranging an innocent man's murder, they remained overly concerned with strict outward rituals.

After talking it over, the priests decided to use the silver to buy a piece of land known as the potter's field. This clay plot was bought at a low price to serve as a graveyard for foreigners who died while visiting Jerusalem. In this way, the payment for Jesus' life provided a burial place for outsiders.

Because the plot was purchased with blood money, the common people named it the Field of Blood. That name was still well known decades later when Matthew wrote his Gospel. The field remained a public, lasting memorial of the leaders' guilt and Jesus' innocence.

These events fulfilled an ancient prophecy about thirty pieces of silver being paid and used to buy a potter's field. The prophet Zechariah had spoken of the shepherd being valued at the price of a common slave, while Jeremiah had written about a potter and buying a field. Matthew showed that even the smallest details of the betrayal and rejection of Jesus took place under God's sovereign plan.

Jesus stood as a prisoner before Pilate, who asked him if he claimed to be the King of the Jews. Jesus answered, 'You have said so,' confirming his royal identity before the Roman ruler. He stood ready to be condemned so that sinners could be freed from guilt.

When the chief priests and elders shouted their accusations against him, Jesus chose not to say a word. He knew their charges were completely false and supported by no real evidence. His calm silence showed his complete innocence and his willing obedience to go to the cross.

Pilate asked Jesus if he could hear the many serious accusations the leaders were pressing against him. The governor was trying to give Jesus a chance to defend himself against charges of treason. He was puzzled that any man facing execution would remain silent.

Jesus refused to answer even a single charge, which left Pilate completely amazed. Roman rulers were accustomed to prisoners pleading, bargaining, or defending themselves with passion. Jesus' quiet dignity fulfilled the ancient prophecy of the suffering servant who remained silent before his shearers.

Every year at the Passover festival, the Roman governor followed a custom of releasing one prisoner chosen by the crowd. This practice helped keep the peace and pleased the Jewish population during a crowded, tense holiday. Pilate hoped to use this custom to free Jesus without directly defying the religious leaders.

At that time, the Romans held a notorious prisoner named Barabbas. He was an infamous criminal who had taken part in an armed rebellion and committed murder. He stood as a clear contrast to Jesus, who had spent his life healing and teaching.

When the crowd gathered before him, Pilate asked them to choose between Barabbas and Jesus, called the Christ. Pilate assumed the people would never prefer an infamous murderer over an innocent teacher. He offered this choice as a way to avoid condemning Jesus himself.

Pilate saw through the rulers' false concern for Roman law and knew they had arrested Jesus out of bitter envy. The priests were jealous of Jesus' popularity, authority, and praise among the people. As an impartial judge, Pilate should have released him immediately, but he hesitated out of political fear.

While Pilate was seated on the official judgment bench, his wife sent him an urgent warning not to harm Jesus. She had suffered terrible distress in a dream that day because of him and recognized that he was a righteous man. God used this warning to testify to Jesus' innocence and caution Pilate against committing a grave injustice.

While Pilate waited, the chief priests and elders moved through the crowd and convinced them to demand Barabbas. They pushed the people to ask for the criminal's release and to call for Jesus' execution. Under their leaders' bad influence, the crowd quickly turned against the one they had recently praised.

When the governor asked the crowd a second time to name which prisoner they wanted, they shouted back for Barabbas. The crowd chose a violent criminal over the holy Son of God. In this dramatic exchange, the innocent Savior took the place of the guilty sinner who deserved to die.

Pilate asked what he should do with Jesus, who was called the Christ. The entire crowd shouted back that he must be crucified. Crucifixion was the most shameful and painful form of Roman execution, showing the terrifying hatred that had taken hold of the mob.
